blocks.text: Before patterns and problems, let's understand what a greedy algorithm actually is and when it works.
A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice at each step without looking ahead or reconsidering past decisions.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406461803-947128902.png
At every step, you look at the available choices, pick the best one right now, and move forward without reconsidering past decisions.
You don’t try all possibilities you trust that the current best choice will lead to a good overall result.
Like a buffet: you pick what looks best at the moment, without planning the whole meal in advance
Brute force means trying every possible solution and picking the best one. You don’t assume anything  you explore all combinations.
DP improves brute force by avoiding repeated work.
It still explores all possibilities, but stores results of subproblems and reuses them.
Greedy takes a different approach it does not try all options.
At each step, it picks the best local choice and moves forward.
Greedy is the fastest but it only works for certain problems.
Two conditions must hold:
Condition 1: Greedy Choice Property
The globally optimal solution can be reached by making locally optimal choices.
This means if you pick the best option at the current step, it will still lead to the overall best (global) solution.

In simple terms:
“Doing the best thing now won’t hurt future decisions.”
But this is not always true. Sometimes a locally good choice can block a better overall solution later that’s when greedy fails.
Condition 2: Optimal Substructure
The optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to its subproblems.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406461805-554414895.png
This means the problem can be broken into smaller parts, and each part also has an optimal solution.

Greedy assumes something stronger than DP:
Once you make a choice, you never need to go back and change it.
Greedy does not always give the correct answer. The classic example:
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406461805-47945765.png
Greedy makes the best choice at each step, but that doesn’t always give the best overall answer.
In this example (making 30 with coins [25, 10, 1]): Greedy picks 25 first because it’s the largest → then keeps using 1 → total 6 coins.
But the optimal solution is different:
Pick 10 three times → total 3 coins, which is clearly better.
Problem: choosing 25 looked best locally, but it blocked a better global solution.

Pick 25 → remaining = 5
Pick 1 → remaining = 4
Pick 1 → remaining = 3
Pick 1 → remaining = 2
Pick 1 → remaining = 1
Pick 1 → remaining = 0
Total coins = 6
Optimal approach:

Pick 10 → remaining = 20
Pick 10 → remaining = 10
Pick 10 → remaining = 0
Total coins = 3
Greedy failed here. It picked 25 greedily, which forced many 1s.
With standard coins [1, 5, 10, 25] greedy works. With arbitrary coins it may not. This is why you need to prove greedy works before using it.
Two standard techniques:
Greedy Stays Ahead
Show that after every step, the greedy solution is at least as good as any other solution at that point.
/engineering/dsa-media/1785406462063-750558645.png
At every step (S1, S2, …), the greedy choice is at least as good (≥) as any other possible choice.
This means greedy is always either equal to or ahead of other approaches at each stage.
It never falls behind at any point.
Because greedy stays ahead throughout all steps, when we finally reach the end (Final), it leads to the optimal solution.
If you’re never behind at any step, you can’t lose in the end
Exchange Argument
Take any optimal solution. Show that you can swap its choices to match the greedy choices without making things worse.
The idea of the exchange argument is to prove that even if an optimal solution starts differently from greedy, we can convert it step by step into the greedy solution without making it worse.
In this example, the optimal solution uses 10 + 10 + 10 (3 coins), while greedy starts with 25.
The key idea is: take the optimal solution and try to replace (exchange) its choices with greedy choices. If swapping doesn’t make the solution worse, then greedy is safe.

But here, if we try to replace a 10 with 25, the solution actually becomes worse (more coins needed). That means we cannot transform the optimal solution into the greedy one without losing quality, so greedy fails for this problem.
In short:

items: If you can swap optimal choices to match greedy without hurting the result → greedy is correct
If you cannot → greedy fails

blocks.text: You want to attend the maximum number of activities without overlap.
Greedy idea: always pick the activity that finishes earliest because it leaves maximum time for the remaining activities.
If you pick an activity that ends late, it blocks many future options. If you pick one that ends early, you keep more choices open.
First, sort activities by their end time:
Start selecting:
Pick (1,3) because it finishes first.

Now find an activity with start ≥ 3.
(2,5) starts before 3, so skip it.
(3,6) starts at 3, so pick it.
Now the last selected activity ends at 6.

Find an activity with start ≥ 6.
(4,7) and (5,8) start before 6, so skip them.
(6,9) starts at 6, so pick it.
No more activities can be selected.

Final answer: (1,3), (3,6), (6,9)
Total = 3 activities
Key idea: pick the earliest finishing activity, then keep selecting the next activity whose start time is at least the end time of the last selected activity.

codes.python:
def max_activities(activities):
    # sort by end time
    activities.sort(key=lambda a: a[1])

    count = 1
    last_end = activities[0][1]

    for i in range(1, len(activities)):
        if activities[i][0] >= last_end:  # starts after last ends
            count += 1
            last_end = activities[i][1]

    return count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    activities = [[1, 3], [2, 5], [4, 7], [1, 8], [5, 9], [8, 10]]
    print(max_activities(activities))

blocks.text: Time Complexity: O(n log n) because we sort the activities by their end time.
After sorting, we scan the list once to pick activities, which takes O(n) time.

So overall:
O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n)
Sorting is the dominating step, so final complexity is O(n log n).
You are given intervals and need to merge all overlapping ones.
Greedy idea: sort by start time and keep merging as long as intervals overlap.
Why this works: once intervals are sorted, any overlap will always happen with the current interval, so you can safely merge step by step.

First, sort by start time:
(1,3), (2,6), (8,10), (9,11)
Start with the first interval (1,3).

Now check the next interval (2,6):
Since 2 ≤ 3, they overlap.
Merge by updating end = max(3,6) = 6
Current interval becomes (1,6)

Next interval (8,10):
Since 8 > 6, no overlap.
Save (1,6) and start a new interval (8,10)

Next interval (9,11):
Since 9 ≤ 10, they overlap.
Merge by updating end = max(10,11) = 11
Current interval becomes (8,11)
No more intervals left.
Final answer: (1,6), (8,11)
Time Complexity: O(n log n) due to sorting, and O(n) for merging. Overall O(n log n).
Key idea: sort by start time, then merge overlapping intervals by extending the current interval.
Time Complexity: O(n log n) sorting the intervals by start time dominates.
After sorting, we traverse the intervals once to merge them, which takes O(n) time.

So overall:
O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n)
Sorting is the dominant step.
Every greedy problem follows the same simple pattern:

Step 1: Decide what choice you need to make at each step
For example: which activity to pick next, or how far you can jump

Step 2: Define the greedy choice
Pick the option that looks best right now
For example: pick the activity that ends earliest, or choose the jump that gives maximum reach

Step 3:  Justify why this choice is safe
The local best choice should lead to a global best answer
For example: ending earliest leaves more room for future activities, maximum reach ensures you don’t miss better positions

Step 4: Apply it efficiently
Sort if required, then process the data in one pass
